blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "Rightly dividing the word of truth." — 2 Timothy 2:15 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Que traza bien la palabra de verdad." — 2 Timoteo 2:15 (RVG)

blocks.en: Note: this method is drawn from the CTS preaching course (WiseSpeak), and much of it will be familiar if you took that course. We give it again here on purpose — to reinforce afresh how to put structure on a sermon before we turn that structure loose on doctrine, unit by unit.
blocks.es_reference: Nota: este método proviene del curso de predicación de CTS (WiseSpeak), y mucho le resultará familiar si tomó aquel curso. Lo repetimos aquí a propósito — para reforzar de nuevo cómo poner estructura a un sermón, antes de soltar esa estructura sobre la doctrina, unidad por unidad.
Día 1 — Del texto a la idea

blocks.en: Unit 1 set the vision; this unit puts the tools in your hand. The doctrinal preacher works with a small set of terms, and learning them is the difference between a sermon that wanders and one that goes somewhere.
blocks.es_reference: La Unidad 1 fijó la visión; esta unidad pone las herramientas en su mano. El predicador doctrinal trabaja con un pequeño conjunto de términos, y aprenderlos es la diferencia entre un sermón que divaga y uno que llega a alguna parte.

blocks.en: Text. The word means “to weave.” The text is the thread on which the whole sermon is woven — the passage of Scripture that is its basis. Idea. The idea is the general topic of the sermon, and it must come from the text, not be carried to it. Donald Miller laid down a rule that has shaped a generation of preachers: the theme of the text and the theme of the sermon must be the same. If they are not, the text is no longer a text — it is a pretext, a starting point for the preacher’s own thoughts.
blocks.es_reference: Texto. La palabra significa “tejer.” El texto es el hilo sobre el cual se teje todo el sermón — el pasaje de la Escritura que es su base. Idea. La idea es el tema general del sermón, y debe venir del texto, no ser llevada al texto. Donald Miller estableció una regla que ha moldeado a una generación de predicadores: el tema del texto y el tema del sermón deben ser el mismo. Si no lo son, el texto deja de ser texto — se vuelve un pretexto, un punto de partida para los propios pensamientos del predicador.

blocks.en: Examples of an idea include faith, the kingdom of God, hope, law, works, love, fasting, baptism, family. Each is a real biblical idea — but each is far too large to preach in one sermon. Try preaching on faith: you could speak of the qualities of faith, the demands of faith, examples of faith, men of faith, or the reasons faith matters — and each of those is itself a full sermon. The idea is the raw quarry stone. It must be cut down before it can be set in a wall.
blocks.es_reference: Ejemplos de una idea: la fe, el reino de Dios, la esperanza, la ley, las obras, el amor, el ayuno, el bautismo, la familia. Cada una es una idea bíblica real — pero cada una es demasiado grande para predicarse en un solo sermón. Intente predicar sobre la fe: podría hablar de las cualidades de la fe, las exigencias de la fe, ejemplos de fe, hombres de fe, o las razones por las que la fe importa — y cada una es ya un sermón completo. La idea es la piedra en bruto de la cantera. Hay que tallarla antes de poder asentarla en el muro.

blocks.en: "Be diligent to present yourself approved to God, a worker who does not need to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth." — 2 Timothy 2:15 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Procura con diligencia presentarte a Dios aprobado... que traza bien la palabra de verdad." — 2 Timoteo 2:15 (RVG)
Día 2 — La pregunta de sondeo (el interrogativo)

blocks.en: Once you have the idea, you ask a question of it. This probing question — the interrogative — is the hinge of the whole method, because the question you ask determines the sermon you will preach. The news writer uses these same questions to produce a story. Rudyard Kipling gave us the easiest way to remember them:
blocks.es_reference: Una vez que tiene la idea, le hace una pregunta. Esta pregunta de sondeo — el interrogativo — es el gozne de todo el método, porque la pregunta que hace determina el sermón que predicará. El periodista usa estas mismas preguntas para producir una nota. Rudyard Kipling nos dio la manera más fácil de recordarlas:

blocks.en:
I keep six honest serving men
(They taught me all I knew);
Their names are What and Why and When
And How and Where and Who.
blocks.es_reference:
Mantengo a seis sirvientes honestos
(me enseñaron todo lo que sabía);
sus nombres son Qué, Por qué, Cuándo,
y Cómo, Dónde y Quién.

blocks.en: For preaching, Kipling’s six become eight by adding which and how much. So the eight interrogatives, and what each one opens up:
blocks.es_reference: Para la predicación, las seis de Kipling se vuelven ocho al añadir cuál y cuánto. Así que los ocho interrogativos, y lo que cada uno abre:
<th>Interrogativo</th><th>Lo que abre</th>
Quiénpersonas
Cuálopciones o alternativas
Quémedios, valor, objetivos
Por quérazones, definiciones, características
Cuándoclases, fases, condiciones
Dóndelugares, fuentes, resultados
Cómosecuencias, maneras
Cuántocantidad, costo, esfuerzo

blocks.en: The probing question is formed by joining the idea to one of these in a full sentence: take the idea of hope and ask, “Who has hope?” or “Which kinds of hope are valid?” or “Why is hope necessary?” Each question is the doorway to a different sermon.
blocks.es_reference: La pregunta de sondeo se forma uniendo la idea a uno de estos en una oración completa: tome la idea de la esperanza y pregunte: “¿Quién tiene esperanza?” o “¿Cuáles esperanzas son válidas?” o “¿Por qué es necesaria la esperanza?” Cada pregunta es la puerta a un sermón distinto.
Día 3 — La palabra clave (el paso generativo)

blocks.en: The keyword arises naturally from the interrogative. It is usually a plural noun, and it is the single most important word in your sermon’s structure — because the keyword is what unites the outline. Every point of the sermon will be one particular instance of the keyword.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra clave surge naturalmente del interrogativo. Suele ser un sustantivo plural, y es la palabra más importante en la estructura de su sermón — porque la palabra clave es lo que une el bosquejo. Cada punto del sermón será un caso particular de la palabra clave.

blocks.en: Three rules govern it. First, it is always plural — almost without exception your keyword ends in ‑s; if it does not, and is not an irregular plural like “people” or “men,” it is probably wrong. Second, only one keyword per sermon, just as you use only one interrogative. Third, avoid generic words like “things.” “Three things about prayer” is not a keyword; it is laziness. The keyword should be as specific as the actual content of your points.
blocks.es_reference: Tres reglas la gobiernan. Primera: siempre es plural — casi sin excepción termina en ‑s; si no, y no es un plural irregular, probablemente está equivocada. Segunda: solo una palabra clave por sermón, así como usa un solo interrogativo. Tercera: evite palabras genéricas como “cosas.” “Tres cosas sobre la oración” no es una palabra clave; es pereza. La palabra clave debe ser tan específica como el contenido real de sus puntos.

blocks.en: Watch one idea — immersion — turn under different questions; the keyword changes, and so does the whole sermon:
blocks.es_reference: Observe una idea — inmersión — girar bajo distintas preguntas; la palabra clave cambia, y con ella todo el sermón:
<th>Interrogativo</th><th>Palabra clave que produce</th>
¿Quién fue sumergido?personas (que fueron sumergidas)
¿Cuáles clases de bautismo?tipos de bautismo
¿Cuáles son sus efectos?efectos (identificación, sujeción, multiplicación)
¿Por qué tenerlo?razones (mandado, modelado, significativo)
¿Cuándo debe hacerse?tiempos
¿Dónde puede hacerse?lugares
¿Cómo se practica?maneras

blocks.en: One idea, seven sermons — and the keyword chose each one. The same thing happens with the idea of faith: people of faith (men who believed God); effects of faith (seeing the invisible, doing the impossible, believing the incredible); times for faith (when discouraged, when distracted, when disappointed); ways we show faith (by word, by walk, by witness); reasons to have faith (for the abundant life, for the eternal life); even amounts of faith (enough to cover our sorrow, enough to fill our lives, enough to move our mountains). One idea, and the interrogative chose the keyword, and the keyword generated a different sermon every time. This is why the interrogative and the keyword together are the generative heart of the method.
blocks.es_reference: Una idea, siete sermones — y la palabra clave eligió cada uno. Lo mismo ocurre con la idea de fe: personas de fe (hombres que creyeron a Dios); efectos de la fe (ver lo invisible, hacer lo imposible, creer lo increíble); tiempos para la fe (cuando desanimados, cuando distraídos, cuando decepcionados); maneras de mostrar fe (por la palabra, por el andar, por el testimonio); razones para tener fe (por la vida abundante, por la vida eterna); aun cantidades de fe (suficiente para cubrir nuestra tristeza, suficiente para llenar nuestra vida, suficiente para mover nuestras montañas). Una idea, y el interrogativo eligió la palabra clave, y la palabra clave generó un sermón distinto cada vez. Por eso el interrogativo y la palabra clave juntos son el corazón generativo del método.

blocks.en: Day 4 — Subject, Objective, and the Two Directions
blocks.es_reference: Día 4 — Tema, objetivo, y las dos direcciones

blocks.en: A clear subject is what keeps a sermon from wandering. I remember walking through the woods with my father as a boy. I would have been hopelessly lost — every tree looked the same — but my father pulled out his compass at intervals; it gave him a fixed point of reference, and we did not wander. The subject of a sermon is its compass.
blocks.es_reference: Un tema claro es lo que impide que un sermón divague. Recuerdo caminar por el bosque con mi padre cuando era niño. Yo me habría perdido sin remedio — cada árbol parecía igual — pero mi padre sacaba su brújula a intervalos; le daba un punto fijo de referencia, y no divagábamos. El tema de un sermón es su brújula.

blocks.en: The subject is the keyword plus a modifier — anything that describes or limits the keyword. Three forms are common: the adjective (“seven deadly sins”), the prepositional phrase (“ways of knowing we have security”), and the subordinate clause (“qualities that God possesses”). The subject answers the question, “What is the sermon about?” Its value is chiefly to the preacher, keeping him aware of his direction; and the people, taking notes, can write the subject at the top of the page and each point beneath it.
blocks.es_reference: El tema es la palabra clave más un modificador — cualquier cosa que describa o limite la palabra clave. Tres formas son comunes: el adjetivo (“siete pecados mortales”), la frase preposicional (“maneras de saber que tenemos seguridad”), y la cláusula subordinada (“cualidades que Dios posee”). El tema responde a la pregunta: “¿De qué trata el sermón?” Su valor es sobre todo para el predicador, manteniéndolo consciente de su rumbo; y la gente, tomando notas, puede escribir el tema al principio de la página y cada punto debajo.

blocks.en: Then comes the objective — the goal of the sermon. It answers a different question: “What do I want people to do?” Phrase it as an action, not a feeling, because right actions carry right beliefs with them. A useful formula begins, “People will…” — “People will respond during the invitation to receive Christ,” or “People will set aside a specific time each day this week for prayer.” Concrete, measurable, and it gives the conclusion a destination.
blocks.es_reference: Luego viene el objetivo — la meta del sermón. Responde a otra pregunta: “¿Qué quiero que la gente haga?” Expréselo como una acción, no un sentimiento, porque las acciones correctas llevan consigo las creencias correctas. Una fórmula útil comienza: “La gente…” — “La gente responderá durante la invitación para recibir a Cristo,” o “La gente apartará un tiempo específico cada día esta semana para la oración.” Concreto, medible, y le da un destino a la conclusión.

blocks.en: Finally, the two directions of movement. Deduction reasons from the general to the specific: begin with a general statement — “God is great” — and break it into specific points (great in His knowledge, great in His power, great in His presence). This is the way of topical preaching. Induction reasons the opposite way, from the specific to the general: begin with the points the text supplies and let them build to the subject. It is something like the game show Jeopardy — the answer is given in the text, and you must find the question. This is the way of textual and expository preaching.
blocks.es_reference: Por último, las dos direcciones del movimiento. La deducción razona de lo general a lo específico: comience con una afirmación general — “Dios es grande” — y divídala en puntos específicos (grande en su conocimiento, grande en su poder, grande en su presencia). Es la vía de la predicación tópica. La inducción razona al revés, de lo específico a lo general: comience con los puntos que el texto provee y deje que construyan el tema. Es algo como el programa Jeopardy — la respuesta está dada en el texto, y usted debe hallar la pregunta. Es la vía del sermón textual y expositivo.

blocks.en: Day 5 — The Method at Work, and the Analysis
blocks.es_reference: Día 5 — El método en acción, y el análisis

blocks.en: Here is the whole method running at once, in a sermon on the doctrine of last things. The idea is the return of Christ; the interrogatives are visible right in the points; each point stands on its own text:
blocks.es_reference: He aquí todo el método corriendo a la vez, en un sermón sobre la doctrina de las últimas cosas. La idea es el regreso de Cristo; los interrogativos están a la vista en los puntos mismos; cada punto se apoya en su propio texto:
<th>Interrogativo → Punto</th><th>Texto base</th>
¿Cuándo? — Nadie sabe el díaMateo 24

blocks.en: What? — What will happen at His coming1 Thessalonians 4
blocks.es_reference: ¿Qué? — Qué sucederá en su venida1 Tesalonicenses 4
¿Qué llegaremos a ser?1 Juan 3:2

blocks.en: The preacher arranged those three points (deduction, topical), yet not one floats free of Scripture — which is the Unit 1 thesis proved in practice. A topical sermon can be every bit as biblical as an expository one, provided every point is anchored in a verse. A Good Friday sermon I have preached more than once shows it: “The Seven Words of the Cross” — idea, the Cross; keyword, words; subject, the seven words of the Cross. A word of pardon (Luke 23:34), a word of promise (Luke 23:43), a word of provision (John 19:26–27), a word of pain (John 19:28), a word of dereliction (Matthew 27:46), a word of triumph (John 19:30), a word of commitment (Luke 23:46). Seven points breaks the usual rule of three to five, so when I preach it I use no subpoints — as a rule, when a sermon has more than three points, drop the subpoints; the people cannot hold a long outline and a layered one at once.
blocks.es_reference: El predicador ordenó esos tres puntos (deducción, tópico), y sin embargo ni uno flota libre de la Escritura — que es la tesis de la Unidad 1 probada en la práctica. Un sermón tópico puede ser tan bíblico como uno expositivo, siempre que cada punto esté anclado en un versículo. Un sermón de Viernes Santo que he predicado más de una vez lo muestra: “Las siete palabras de la Cruz” — idea, la Cruz; palabra clave, palabras; tema, las siete palabras de la Cruz. Una palabra de perdón (Lucas 23:34), una de promesa (Lucas 23:43), una de provisión (Juan 19:26–27), una de dolor (Juan 19:28), una de desamparo (Mateo 27:46), una de triunfo (Juan 19:30), una de entrega (Lucas 23:46). Siete puntos rompe la regla usual de tres a cinco, así que cuando lo predico no uso subpuntos — por regla, cuando un sermón tiene más de tres puntos, deje caer los subpuntos; la gente no puede sostener a la vez un bosquejo largo y uno en capas.

blocks.en: Two of Cook’s working maxims name the difference between the inductive forms. In the textual sermon the points come from the text but the preacher supplies the explanation — the text supplies the skeleton; the preacher supplies the flesh. In the expository sermon both the points and their explanation come from the text — the preacher is the messenger; the text is the message.
blocks.es_reference: Dos máximas de Cook nombran la diferencia entre las formas inductivas. En el sermón textual los puntos vienen del texto pero el predicador aporta la explicación — el texto provee el esqueleto; el predicador aporta la carne. En el sermón expositivo tanto los puntos como su explicación vienen del texto — el predicador es el mensajero; el texto es el mensaje.

blocks.en: Finally, a preaching analysis is the reverse exercise: going through a text by induction to discover its interrogatives and keywords. It is not the same as an outline of the chapter; it begins with a question and contains the subject of the passage. Master the analysis and you can preach any text in the Book. Unit 3 begins applying all of this, doctrine by doctrine, starting with Revelation.
blocks.es_reference: Por último, un análisis de predicación es el ejercicio inverso: recorrer un texto por inducción para descubrir sus interrogativos y palabras clave. No es lo mismo que un bosquejo del capítulo; comienza con una pregunta y contiene el tema del pasaje. Domina el análisis y podrás predicar cualquier texto del Libro. La Unidad 3 comienza a aplicar todo esto, doctrina por doctrina, empezando con la Revelación.
"¡Predica la palabra!" — 2 Timoteo 4:2 (RVG)

The probing question asked of the idea is called the ____, and it is the hinge of the whole method.
The easiest way to remember the six questions of the news writer was given to us by the poet Rudyard ____.
The keyword is usually a noun in the ____ form, almost always ending in -s.
Avoid generic keywords such as "____"; the keyword should be as specific as the content of your points.
The subject of a sermon is its ____, a fixed point of reference that keeps it from wandering.

sa.prompt: Define “text” and “idea,” and explain how they must relate.
sa.model: The text is the passage of Scripture on which the sermon is based; the word itself means to weave, and the text is the thread the sermon is woven upon. The idea is the general topic or theme of the sermon. The two must relate in one strict way: the idea must come from the text, so that the theme of the text and the theme of the sermon are the same. If they differ, the text has become only a pretext, a mere starting point for the preacher’s own notions rather than the Word he is bound to preach.

sa.prompt: What is an interrogative, and how does it move the preacher toward a keyword? Give an example.
sa.model: An interrogative is the probing question the preacher asks of the idea, such as who, which, what, why, when, where, how, or how much. It is the hinge of the method because the question chosen determines the sermon. The interrogative moves toward a keyword because the answer to the question is naturally a plural noun, and that noun becomes the keyword from which the outline grows. For example, taking the idea of immersion and asking “Why have it?” yields the keyword reasons — commanded, modeled, meaningful — and those become the points.

sa.prompt: Define the keyword. What makes a good one, and what should you avoid?
sa.model: The keyword is usually a plural noun that arises from the interrogative, and from it the whole outline is derived, since each point of the sermon is one instance of the keyword. A good keyword is as specific as possible, so that it genuinely controls and shapes the points. What you should avoid is a vague, empty word such as “things,” which gives the outline no real direction. The more precise the keyword, the clearer and stronger the sermon that grows from it.

sa.prompt: Explain the “subject”: what it includes and what question it answers.
sa.model: The subject is the focal idea of the sermon, and it includes the keyword plus a modifier, which is often a prepositional phrase — for example, “ways of knowing we have security,” where ways is the keyword and the rest is the modifier. It answers the question, “What is the sermon about?” Its value is chiefly to the preacher, because it keeps him aware of the exact direction of the sermon and guards him from wandering off the point he set out to make.

sa.prompt: Walk through the whole method from idea to outline, using immersion or another doctrine as your example.
sa.model: The method runs in order. You begin with an idea drawn from the text, say immersion. You ask an interrogative of it, for example “Why have it?” That question yields a keyword, here reasons. The keyword plus a modifier forms the subject, “reasons for immersion.” The keyword then generates the outline, so each point is one reason — commanded, modeled, meaningful — and each point is anchored to its own text. The whole movement from a general subject down to specific points is deduction, the way of topical preaching, yet it stays biblical because every point rests on Scripture.

sa.prompt: Distinguish deduction and induction, and tell which sermon types use each.
sa.model: Deduction moves from the general to the specific: the preacher begins with a general subject and divides it into its specific points. This is the process of topical preaching. Induction moves the opposite way, from the specific to the general: the preacher begins with the particular points the text supplies and lets them build up to the general subject. This is the process of textual and expository preaching. So the difference is the direction of travel, and each direction belongs to its own family of sermons.

sa.prompt: What is a preaching analysis, and how is it different from an outline of the passage?
sa.model: A preaching analysis is the work of going through a text by induction to discover the interrogatives and keywords hidden in it. It is different from an ordinary outline of the passage in that an outline merely lists what the chapter says, while an analysis begins with a question and contains the subject of the passage. The analysis is aimed at preaching: it does not just describe the text but draws out the questions and keywords from which sermons can actually be built.

sa.prompt: Take one doctrine and show how two different interrogatives produce two different keywords, and so two different sermons.
sa.model: Take the doctrine of immersion as the idea. Ask one interrogative, “What are its effects?” and the keyword is effects, giving a sermon whose points are identification, subjugation, and multiplication. Ask a different interrogative of the very same idea, “Why have it?” and the keyword becomes reasons, giving a different sermon whose points are commanded, modeled, and meaningful. The idea never changed; the interrogative chose the keyword, and the keyword generated two distinct outlines. This is why the interrogative and keyword are the generative heart of the method.

sa.prompt: Why must the subject of the sermon be the subject of the text?
sa.model: The subject of the sermon must be the subject of the text because that is what keeps the sermon biblical rather than merely the preacher’s own opinion. If the idea is drawn from the text, the preacher is proclaiming the Word; if it is brought to the text from outside, the text becomes a pretext and the authority of the sermon collapses into the authority of the man. The text must govern the idea, not the reverse, so that what the people hear is what God said and not what the preacher wished to say.

sa.prompt: Summarize the method of Unit 2 in your own words, from idea to finished outline.
sa.model: The method of Unit 2 moves in clear steps. The preacher draws an idea from the text, then asks an interrogative of that idea. The interrogative yields a keyword, usually a plural noun, and the keyword joined to a modifier forms the subject. From the keyword the outline is derived, each point being one instance of it, and each point is anchored to its own text. Whether the preacher reasons from the general down to the points by deduction or from the points up to the subject by induction, the method keeps the sermon both ordered and biblical.
